steps.label: Choosing the cost function
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp09 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 10 pages; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Two faults
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP09. Prerequisites: the sigmoid and the backpropagation δ (KP06), probability with ln turning a product into a sum, and Bayes' theorem (chapter 2). The squared error has two faults. It is unfair: errors are squared before they are summed, so large errors dominate; errors of 0.9 and 0.1 differ 9 times, but squared they are 0.81 and 0.01, which differ 81 times. It gets stuck: at the extreme, target 1 and output 0.001, the squared error is only 0.499 and stops growing, so gradient descent can get stuck; the other loss, minus ln ŷ, is 6.908 at ŷ equal to 0.001 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the plateau.

steps.label: Plateau
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the two faults of the squared error. This page shows how small δ gets. A plateau is a flat region where the cost is large but the gradient is almost 0, so gradient descent hardly moves on it. For a single sigmoid output with squared error, δ equals (y minus ŷ) times ŷ times (1 minus ŷ); the closer ŷ is to 0 or 1, the smaller the slope ŷ(1 minus ŷ), which squeezes even a large error into a small signal. With target y equal to 1 and net equal to minus 10, ŷ is 0.000045, the error is near 1 and δ is only 0.000045; only a small middle stretch of the curve is large and both sides are plateaus (computed by program). Next, the next page covers cross-entropy.

steps.label: Cross-entropy
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the plateau. This page switches to the cross-entropy. The cross-entropy treats the output ŷ as the probability that the target is 1: J equals minus (y ln ŷ plus (1 minus y) ln (1 minus ŷ)), which for y equal to 1 is minus ln ŷ. The derivation, step by step: one, the partial derivative of J with respect to ŷ is minus (y minus ŷ) over ŷ(1 minus ŷ); two, the sigmoid slope is ŷ(1 minus ŷ); three, multiplying by the chain rule, ŷ(1 minus ŷ) cancels exactly and δ equals y minus ŷ. The sign follows KP06; the source writes ŷ minus y, a sign apart. On the right is the comparison for y equal to 1: for net equal to minus 10, minus 5, minus 2, 0, 2, 5 the squared-error δ is 0.00005, 0.00660, 0.09248, 0.12500, 0.01252, 0.00004 and the cross-entropy δ is 1.0000, 0.9933, 0.8808, 0.5000, 0.1192, 0.0067 (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the training comparison.

steps.label: Training comparison
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on cross-entropy. This page compares training. The setup is my own design, implemented in a program: one sigmoid neuron ŷ equal to σ(b plus wx), four points x equal to minus 2, minus 1, 1, 2 with targets 0, 0, 1, 1; the start is w equal to minus 3 and b equal to 0, all four wrong; η equals 0.5 with batch updates using the mean δ of the four points per epoch; all right means that the number of points where ŷ above 0.5 agrees with the target is 4. Result: cross-entropy gets all four right in 5 epochs and the squared error needs 85. The common myth is that only the cross-entropy gets it right; in fact both costs end up right, and the difference is the speed from a badly wrong start (computed by program). Next, the next page covers likelihood.

steps.label: Likelihood
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the training comparison. This page explains why the cross-entropy is the right cost. The likelihood is the probability of observing this data if the model is right; larger is better, and independent samples multiply. Example: outputs 0.9, 0.8, 0.3, 0.1 with targets 1, 1, 0, 0. The probabilities of the targets are 0.9, 0.8, 1 minus 0.3 equal to 0.7, and 1 minus 0.1 equal to 0.9; the product 0.9 times 0.8 times 0.7 times 0.9 is 0.4536 and minus ln 0.4536 is 0.7905; the four cross-entropies 0.105, 0.223, 0.357, 0.105 also sum to 0.7905, the same. So minimizing the cross-entropy is maximizing the likelihood (computed by program). Next, the next page covers softmax.

steps.label: softmax
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on likelihood. This page handles several classes. The softmax is used for several classes: ŷk equals e to the vk over the sum of e to the vk', every output lies between 0 and 1 and they sum to exactly 1. Example with v equal to (2, 1, 0.1): e squared is 7.389, e to the 1 is 2.718 and e to the 0.1 is 1.105, total 11.212; ŷ equals (0.659, 0.242, 0.099). With target y equal to (1, 0, 0): J equals minus ln 0.659, which is 0.417. The δk needed by backpropagation equals yk minus ŷk, that is (0.341, minus 0.242, minus 0.099), the same as numerical differences (checked by program). Next, the next page covers discriminative learning.

steps.label: Discriminative learning
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on softmax. This page looks at discriminative learning: since the goal is to lower the classification error, put the focus directly on the largest posterior probability and push the decision surface to reduce the errors. The contrast example is my own design, implemented in a program: x equal to minus 3, minus 2, minus 1 are class 0, and x equal to 1, 2, 3 plus the outlier x equal to 40 are class 1. For the squared error use the least-squares line y approximately a x plus b with a equal to 0.0165 and b equal to 0.477 and cut where the line equals 0.5, at 1.40, so x equal to 1 is misclassified. For the cross-entropy use one sigmoid output with gradient descent from 0, η equal to 0.5 and 20000 rounds; the cut is near 0 and all seven are right. The contrast changes both the output and the cost; the error rate itself is not differentiable, so a smooth version is used, with the risk of local minima (computed by program). Next, the next page covers Bayesian training.

steps.label: Bayesian training
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on discriminative learning. This page looks at Bayesian training: put a prior p(w) on the weights, and when data arrive Bayes' theorem gives the posterior p(w given Y) equal to p(Y given w) times p(w) over p(Y); when classifying, average over all w, the integral of φk(x; w) times the posterior. The example is my own design, computed with Gaussian formulas: prior w follows N(0, 2 squared); every sample says w is about 1.5 with noise standard deviation 1; n samples. The posterior precision, the inverse of the variance, equals 1/4 plus n and the posterior mean equals 1.5n over (1/4 plus n). For n equal to 0, 1, 5, 20 the posterior standard deviation is 2, 0.894, 0.436, 0.222 and the posterior mean is 0, 1.2, 1.43, 1.48. The price is that high-dimensional integrals are expensive; the source warns that in practice replacing least squares does not necessarily bring a real improvement (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the worse the start.

steps.label: Worse starts
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on Bayesian training. This is the extension: the worse the start. With the data of page 4, η equal to 0.5 and b equal to 0, for start w equal to minus 1, minus 2, minus 3, minus 4, minus 6, minus 8, minus 10 the squared error needs 11, 31, 85, 227, 1631, 11950, 88141 epochs and the cross-entropy needs 2, 4, 5, 6, 9, 12, 14. The squared-error δ shrinks exponentially as the start gets worse, so its epoch count grows roughly exponentially; the cross-entropy δ stays near 1 and its epoch count is almost flat. Both costs end up right and the difference is the speed from a badly wrong start (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the worse the start. Two exercises: a single sigmoid output, target 1, net equal to minus 4. Q1: ŷ equals σ(minus 4), which is 1 over (1 plus e to the 4th) and equals 0.0180. Q2: the squared-error δ equals 0.9820 times 0.0180 times 0.9820, which is 0.01735; the cross-entropy δ equals 1 minus ŷ, which is 0.9820; the ratio 0.9820 over 0.01735 is 56.6. Check: the ratio is 1 over ŷ(1 minus ŷ), larger when the output is more extreme; about 22000 at net equal to minus 10 (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
